metadata.title: The one-parameter fix that proves the confidence was decorative
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: why does a single learned temperature parameter prove deep network confidence was decorative? Lands the carry-out that if dividing by one learned number fixes the probabilities without altering a single decision, the original confidence was decorative all along.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B07 (Logits and softmax bar chart softening as temperature dial turns)
metadata.one_flag: B10 — reliability diagram before and after T

beats.narration_text: When a deep neural network outputs ninety-nine percent confidence, you might assume that number reflects genuine certainty. But modern classifiers are notoriously overconfident. A single learned number can fix it without changing a single decision. Let's see why.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types naive question, hesitates on "real?", corrects to "decorative?"

props.text:
When a deep network
states 99% confidence,
is the probability
real?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per course-skepticism SKILL.md. Writer types naive question, hesitates, corrects to misconception. Liam reads over typing animation.

beats.narration_text: Deep neural networks routinely output extreme confidence scores. They say ninety-nine percent certain with crisp, unwavering precision.

shot.new_visual_element: Model output card: Dog 99.1% with crisp precision

production_viz.label: The 99% Claim
production_viz.mechanic: Classifier output card showing 99.1% top prediction and crisp confidence badge.

beats.narration_text: Yet when you evaluate thousands of predictions where the model claimed ninety-nine percent, the true empirical accuracy is often only eighty-five percent. The network is fundamentally miscalibrated.

shot.new_visual_element: The 14-point overconfidence gap: 99% stated vs 85% empirical

production_viz.label: The Overconfidence Gap
production_viz.mechanic: Comparison cards revealing the 14% gap between stated probability and observed empirical accuracy.

beats.narration_text: To see where this comes from, look at the network's final layer. The model computes unnormalized scores called logits, then passes them through a softmax function to turn them into probabilities.

shot.new_visual_element: Logits entering standard Softmax, producing extreme probability bars

production_viz.label: Logits to Softmax
production_viz.mechanic: The Visual Object: raw unnormalized logits mapped through softmax into an extreme probability bar chart.

beats.narration_text: Intuition assumes that confidence and correctness are inseparable: that if a model is ninety-nine percent sure, flattening that number would break its ability to pick the right answer.

shot.new_visual_element: Naive lock: Confidence bound inextricably to Correctness

production_viz.label: The Inseparability Illusion
production_viz.mechanic: Naive assumption diagram showing confidence locked to classification correctness.

beats.narration_text: In 2017, Guo, Pleiss, Sun, and Weinberger proved that assumption wrong. A network's ranking of options is usually fine. It picked the right class; only its stated certainty was inflated.

shot.new_visual_element: Guo et al. ICML 2017 finding: Ranking preserved, stated certainty inflated

production_viz.label: The Guo Finding
production_viz.mechanic: Empirical discovery: relative class rankings are correct, but absolute confidence scale is distorted.

beats.narration_text: Their fix was surprisingly simple: temperature scaling. Before computing the softmax, you divide every logit by a single learned number, T. When T is greater than one, it gently cools the distribution.

shot.new_visual_element: Softmax formula with temperature scalar T > 1.0

production_viz.label: Temperature Scaling Equation
production_viz.mechanic: Formula softmax(z / T) with dial T > 1.0 cooling the exponent.

beats.narration_text: Here is the visual payoff. As temperature T turns up, watch the probabilities slosh and spread. The peaked ninety-nine percent bar softens outward into neighbouring classes, settling right at eighty-five percent.

shot.new_visual_element: Manim move: slosh/spread — 99% bar softens outward as T increases

production_viz.label: Anchor Payoff: Slosh / Spread
production_viz.mechanic: Manim move slosh/spread: 99% bar softens and redistributes to neighbouring bars as T increases from 1.0 to 2.2.

beats.narration_text: Because dividing by a positive constant is strictly monotonic, it cannot alter the order of the logits. The highest score stays highest. Not a single decision or top-one classification changes.

production_viz.label: Monotonic Invariance
production_viz.mechanic: Mathematical proof: argmax(z / T) == argmax(z). Ranking order is strictly preserved.

beats.narration_text: That is the core insight. If you can fix the probabilities across an entire dataset with one global dial without changing a single decision, the original confidence score was decorative all along.

shot.new_visual_element: Decoupling tracks: Decisions 100% stable vs Confidence re-scaled

production_viz.label: The Decorative Confidence Proof
production_viz.mechanic: Decoupling diagram showing decision track untouched while confidence track is un-decorated.

beats.narration_text: One flag: check the reliability diagram before and after. At temperature one, the curve sags far below the diagonal in the overconfident tail. Scaled by T, the curve hugs the honest forty-five-degree line.

shot.new_visual_element: Reliability diagram: T=1.0 overconfident curve vs T=2.2 calibrated diagonal

production_viz.label: Reliability Diagram Diagnostic
production_viz.mechanic: Reliability diagram showing empirical accuracy vs stated confidence before and after temperature scaling.

beats.narration_text: In one direction, temperature scaling delivers real value. On in-distribution data, it turns an arbitrary number into a calibrated probability you can use for risk management.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction A: In-distribution calibration yields honest risk estimates

production_viz.label: Direction A: Calibrated In-Distribution
production_viz.mechanic: Card showing in-distribution validity: probabilities now match empirical risk frequencies.

beats.narration_text: In the other direction, temperature scaling is not magic: if the deployment distribution drifts from your calibration set, that honest number goes stale silently.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction B: Distribution shift caveat — honest numbers go stale silently

production_viz.label: Direction B: Distribution Shift Caveat
production_viz.mechanic: Card illustrating distribution shift caveat: calibration is distribution-bound and degrades under domain drift.

beats.narration_text: If dividing by one learned number fixes the probabilities without altering a single decision, the original confidence was decorative all along.

props.quote: If dividing by one learned number fixes the probabilities without altering a single decision, the original confidence was decorative all along.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Take a classifier in your pipeline with a softmax output. Measure its empirical accuracy in the top confidence bin. If your ninety-nine percent predictions only succeed eighty-five percent of the time, fit a single temperature parameter T on held-out logits and verify that the ranking never changes. Liam, in for Bear.

props.command: Measure classifier accuracy at top confidence bin. If 99% predictions hit 85%, fit temperature parameter T and verify ranking is unchanged.
